title: Littering: Not Cool
summary: Josh and Chuck open with plugs for Lethal Lit season two (Josh's voice role) and Joe Randazzo's Dr. Sex Reese, then examine littering. They cover the etymology of "litter" (from an old French/Middle English word for a portable bed, and farm scattering of hay bedding), the postwar rise of disposable packaging and the decline of reuse (milk bottles, canister chips, bottled water jugs), Vermont's early bottle bill, and the founding and tactics of Keep America Beautiful, which they frame as a greenwashing effort to shift responsibility to individuals. They discuss the Crying Indian PSA (Iron Eyes Cody, who was not Native American), Woodsy the Owl, and anti-litter and dumping laws. Statistics from the 2009 Keep America Beautiful roadside study (about 51.2 billion pieces of litter, cigarette butts most common) and a 2020-era follow-up are covered, along with behavioral research showing litter begets litter and that seeing someone litter in a clean place makes people less likely to litter. They discuss organic litter (apple cores, banana peels, Grand Canyon decomposition study), harm to wildlife, cigarette butt toxicity, plogging, and bottle deposit laws. The episode ends with a listener mail item about the funny bone sensation during massages, answered by a physical therapist, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and podcast plugs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug Lethal Lit season two, in which Josh did a voice role, and Joe Randazzo's show Dr. Sex Reese. They joke about a listener voicemail and Chuck's voice-acting experience, then introduce the littering topic.

segments.title: Etymology of litter
segments.summary: The word litter traces to an Old French/Middle English term for a portable bed with two poles, and separately to farmers scattering straw as animal bedding. The sense of scattered trash came later, with an eighteenth-century literary usage cited.

segments.title: Reuse culture and postwar disposable packaging
segments.summary: Before the fifties, Americans reused most goods: milk bottles returned to the milkman, canister potato chips, and reusable water jugs. After World War II, wartime packaging technology enabled cheap disposables, and industry pushed throwaway packaging. Littering became more common, and Vermont farmers complained about discarded bottles.

segments.title: Vermont bottle bill
segments.summary: Vermont passed an early bottle bill banning throwaway bottles, which alarmed the beverage industry and prompted a response.

segments.title: Formation of Keep America Beautiful and greenwashing
segments.summary: Beverage and packaging companies including Dixie Cup, Coca-Cola, Owens-Illinois, and American Can formed Keep America Beautiful to fight bottle bills by promoting individual responsibility against littering. The hosts call it greenwashing that diverted attention from disposable packaging. In 1974 the group opposed a California bottle bill, a leaked comment called supporters communists, and environmental groups left.

segments.title: Crying Indian PSA, Woodsy the Owl and litter laws
segments.summary: The 1971 Crying Indian ad starred Iron Eyes Cody, who was actually Sicilian American, and the hosts critique its portrayal. They mention Woodsy the Owl and discuss anti-litter and dumping laws, including fines and penalties and uneven enforcement.

segments.title: Litter statistics and cigarette butts
segments.summary: The 2009 Keep America Beautiful roadside study counted about 51.2 billion pieces of litter, around 67 per mile, with cigarette butts the most common. Paper, plastic, metal, and glass shares are covered. A pandemic-year follow-up showed declines.

segments.title: Organic litter, wildlife harm and cigarette toxicity
segments.summary: Apple cores and banana peels persist, as a Grand Canyon study showed, and feeding wildlife is harmful. About a million animals a year are estimated to die from litter. A single cigarette butt in water killed half the fish in a test, and herbal biodegradable cigarette butts exist but have not caught on.

segments.title: Littering psychology and cleanup solutions
segments.summary: Survey and observation research found many people litter even near trash cans, and littering is contagious: people litter more in littered spaces and less in clean ones. Cleanup volunteering, plogging, and bottle deposit laws are suggested, with the conclusion that addressing disposable packaging supply matters.

segments.title: Listener mail: funny bone and massage
segments.summary: A physical therapist explains why Chuck's hand curls when a massage therapist presses his forearm muscle belly, due to tendon length-tension relationships, and distinguishes cubital tunnel syndrome from tennis elbow.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, asking listeners to send mail and noting the show is an iHeart production.
